kw: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
lede: A Dublin boy who left Ireland at twenty-two and never came back to live, then spent the rest of his life rebuilding the city street by street on paper, until a single ordinary Thursday in June 1904 became the most famous day in modern literature.

ps: James Augustine Aloysius Joyce was born in Rathgar, Dublin, on 2 February 1882, the eldest surviving child of a large family that slid steadily into poverty.

He left Ireland in 1904 with Nora Barnacle and lived in Trieste, Zurich and Paris. From abroad he wrote Dubliners (1914), A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916), Ulysses (1922) and Finnegans Wake (1939).

Ulysses follows a few Dubliners through one day, 16 June 1904, and changed what a novel could do. Joyce died in Zurich on 13 January 1941, aged 58, the same year as Virginia Woolf, who was born the same year he was.
His father, John Joyce, was a charming, hard-drinking tax collector who lost his post and moved the family from house to house, each one cheaper than the last. Ten children survived infancy.

James was sent at six to Clongowes Wood College, a Jesuit boarding school, and later to Belvedere College in Dublin, also Jesuit, where he won prizes for essays. The Jesuits gave him a love of exact language and argument, and the Catholic faith he later abandoned.

At University College Dublin he studied modern languages, taught himself Norwegian to read Ibsen, and published a review of Ibsen's last play in a London magazine at eighteen. Ibsen sent his thanks through his translator, William Archer.
He went to Paris in 1902, but was called home in 1903 because his mother was dying. She died in August 1903.
16 June 1904. He went walking with Nora Barnacle, a chambermaid from Galway, for the first time. He later set Ulysses on that date.

Exile, October 1904. He and Nora left Dublin together, unmarried. He found work teaching English at the Berlitz school in Pola, then in Trieste, where their children Giorgio (1905) and Lucia (1907) were born.

Dubliners, 1914. The book of stories was accepted in 1906 but publishers feared real place names and rough language. One Dublin printer destroyed the sheets in 1912. It finally came out in London in June 1914.
A Portrait, 1914 to 1916. Ezra Pound got it serialised in the London magazine The Egoist. It appeared as a book in New York in December 1916.
Zurich, 1915 to 1920. The First World War pushed the family to neutral Switzerland. Joyce wrote much of Ulysses there, and his eye troubles worsened.
The Little Review, 1918 to 1921. Episodes of Ulysses appeared in an American magazine until its editors were prosecuted and convicted of obscenity in New York in 1921.
Paris, 2 February 1922. Sylvia Beach, an American who ran the bookshop Shakespeare and Company, published Ulysses on his fortieth birthday, in a first edition of 1,000 copies.
Finnegans Wake, 1939. After seventeen years of work under the title 'Work in Progress', his last book appeared in May 1939.
Zurich, 1941. Fleeing occupied France at the end of 1940, the family returned to Zurich. He died there after an operation for a perforated ulcer and is buried in the Fluntern cemetery.
Dubliners (1914): fifteen stories of what Joyce called the 'paralysis' of the city, from a boy's disappointment in 'Araby' to the long, snow-covered last story, 'The Dead'.

A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916): the growth of Stephen Dedalus, a thinly veiled young Joyce, whose language grows up with him, from baby talk to the voice of a young man who decides to leave Ireland to become a writer.

Ulysses (1922): eighteen episodes loosely shaped on Homer's Odyssey. Leopold Bloom, a Jewish advertising salesman, wanders Dublin; Stephen Dedalus wanders too; Bloom's wife Molly stays home. Each episode is written in a different style, including newspaper headlines, a play script and a mock history of English prose. It ends with Molly's long unpunctuated thoughts, closing on 'Yes'.
Finnegans Wake (1939): a night's dream in a language built from puns in dozens of languages. It gave physicists the word 'quark'.
He also wrote poems, Chamber Music (1907) and Pomes Penyeach (1927), and one play, Exiles (1918).

Nora Barnacle (1884 to 1951), his companion for 37 years. She did not read much of his work but was its deepest source; Molly Bloom owes her a great deal. They married in London in 1931, for the children's inheritance.
Stanislaus Joyce (1884 to 1955), his younger brother, who followed him to Trieste and kept the family afloat with loans and patience.
Lucia Joyce (1907 to 1982), his daughter, a dancer, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia in the 1930s and spent most of her life in care. Joyce never stopped hoping she would recover.
Ezra Pound (1885 to 1972), the American poet who found him publishers and patrons.
Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876 to 1961), an English editor who gave him money for years so that he could write.
Sylvia Beach (1887 to 1962), who risked her small bookshop to publish Ulysses.
Samuel Beckett (1906 to 1989), a young Irish writer in Paris who helped him with Finnegans Wake from 1928 and remained a devoted friend.

Joyce's Dublin was a city of the British Empire, poor, Catholic and argumentative, dreaming of Home Rule. He left before the 1916 Rising, the war of independence and the creation of the Irish Free State in 1922, the year Ulysses appeared.
Trieste, where he spent eleven years, was the Austro-Hungarian Empire's great port: Italian, German, Slovene and Jewish. Some of Bloom comes from people he met there.

Paris in the 1920s was full of exiles and experiment: Pound, Hemingway, Gertrude Stein, Picasso and Stravinsky. Ulysses, with T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land of the same year, became the landmark of literary modernism.
Virginia Woolf, his exact contemporary, read Ulysses with mixed admiration and irritation. Her Hogarth Press had turned it down in 1918, partly because no printer would touch it.
Ulysses is regularly named the most important novel in English of the twentieth century. Its methods, such as following a character's thoughts directly, are now part of ordinary fiction.
Bloomsday, 16 June, was first marked by a group of Dublin writers in 1954 and is now celebrated around the world with readings, Edwardian costumes and breakfasts of kidneys, as Bloom ate.
Dublin, which once disapproved of him, now has his statue on North Earl Street, a James Joyce Centre and a Joyce tower museum at Sandycove, where Ulysses begins.

myths.t: In the United States it was treated as obscene, and copies were seized and burned, until Judge John Woolsey ruled on 6 December 1933 that it was not pornographic. Random House published it in 1934. Britain allowed it in 1936.

myths.c: Joyce wrote whatever came into his head.
myths.t: He worked with huge care, with charts, notebooks and schedules. He once joked that he had put in enough puzzles to keep the professors busy for centuries.
Not fully, but nearly at times. He suffered from glaucoma, cataracts and painful eye inflammation, had about a dozen operations, and often wrote with huge letters and magnifying glasses.
He criticised it fiercely and chose exile, but he wrote about almost nothing else, and asked visitors for the smallest details of Dublin streets and shops.
